notes.meaning: Joab noticed that King David still cared deeply for his exiled son Absalom. Even though David had been angry over Amnon's murder, he missed his son and wished he could return. Joab began looking for a way to bring Absalom home without hurting David's reputation for justice.

Joab sent for a clever woman from Tekoa, a town several miles south of Jerusalem. He instructed her to dress in dark mourning clothes and look like someone who had been grieving a death for a very long time. Her appearance was designed to catch David's eye and soften his heart.

Joab told the woman exactly what story to tell the king. He wanted her to present a pretend family problem so David would make a ruling without knowing it applied to his own household. This was similar to the way the prophet Nathan had once caught David off guard with a parable.

The woman bowed low before David with her face to the ground and cried out for royal help. In Israel, ordinary citizens who felt denied justice could appeal straight to the king. Her desperate cry gained the king's full attention.

David asked her what was wrong, and she replied that she was a poor widow whose husband had died. Widows in Bible times had very little protection and often relied entirely on the ruler's mercy. Her status invited David to act as a protector for the weak.

She claimed her two sons got into a sudden brawl in an open field where nobody was around to separate them. In the heat of the fight, one son struck down the other and killed him. Her tale mirrored Absalom killing Amnon, but made it sound like an accidental fight rather than planned murder.

The woman told David that her entire clan wanted to execute the surviving son to avenge the brother's blood. She pleaded that if they put him to death, her last burning coal would be put out, leaving her dead husband without any family name on earth. She made it sound as if the relatives cared more about taking her land than doing justice.
David told the woman to return home and promised to give orders regarding her case. He was moved by her story and was willing to step in and protect her family.

The woman said that if letting her son live broke God's law, any guilt should fall on her and her father's house, leaving the king blameless. She said this to remove any hesitation David might have about shielding a killer. Her words pushed the king to make an immediate, firm decision.
David declared that if anyone tried to bother her about the matter, she should bring them straight to him. He used his royal authority to promise that no one would dare lay a hand on her or her son.

The woman pressed David to seal his promise by making a vow in the name of the Lord. David gave a solemn oath that not a single hair from her son's head would fall to the ground. Without realizing it, David had officially bound himself to choose family mercy over strict punishment.
Having locked the king into a sworn promise, the woman politely asked permission to say one more word. David allowed her to speak, not knowing that she was about to turn the trap on him.

The woman directly challenged David, asking why he would treat God's people differently than he had just promised to treat her. By keeping his own banished son away from home, the king stood convicted by his own judgment. She argued that the whole nation wanted Absalom back just as much as she wanted her son spared.

She reminded David that every person must die and that life cannot be recovered, like water poured out on dry dirt. Yet God Himself is merciful and devises ways to bring back those who are separated from Him. In Christian teaching, this verse shows how God makes a way through Christ to welcome banished sinners back into His family.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The traditional Catholic Douay-Rheims version translates this verse as God not willing any soul to perish, but calling back the one who has been cast out.

notes.meaning: The woman circled back to her own story, claiming she came because the people around her had made her terrified for her son's life. She told the king she had hoped his royal mercy would grant her petition.

She expressed confidence that the king would listen and protect both her and her son from being cut off from God's land. In Israel, the land was God's special gift, and being cast out meant losing the blessing of worshipping among His people.

She praised David, saying his word would bring peace because he had wisdom like an angel of God to tell good from evil. She closed her request by praying that the Lord would remain with him as he governed.
David realized that this clever appeal was too well constructed for an ordinary country widow to make on her own. He told her not to hide anything from him and prepared to ask her an honest question.

David asked the woman whether his army commander Joab was the real force behind her story. The woman confessed immediately, telling the king that he hit the mark perfectly and that Joab had indeed given her every line to say.

The woman explained that Joab had staged the whole event to bring about a change in Absalom's situation. She showered David with flattery, saying he was as wise as an angel who knew everything going on across the land.
David spoke to Joab, who was standing nearby, and told him that his plan had succeeded. He officially granted the request and ordered Joab to go and fetch the young man Absalom back home.
Joab fell facedown to thank and bless the king for granting his desire. He felt he had secured great favor with David by successfully pleading for the royal prince.
Joab lost no time and traveled northeast to Geshur, where Absalom had been living in exile with his grandfather. He escorted Absalom back to the city of Jerusalem.

David set a strict limit by commanding that Absalom go straight to his own house without ever seeing the king's face. David wanted to show the public that he still hated the crime of murder and could not easily welcome Absalom back. This partial forgiveness left the relationship damaged and father and son still distant.

Absalom was celebrated across all Israel for his stunning good looks, having no physical blemish from head to toe. His charming appearance won the hearts of the people, even though his character was deeply flawed. Physical beauty does not mean a person has a pure heart before God.

Absalom grew an unusually heavy head of hair and cut it only when it became too uncomfortable, weighing it at about five pounds by the royal standard. He took great personal pride in this feature, displaying his hair as a sign of strength and beauty. In the end, his magnificent hair would contribute to his violent death.

Absalom had three sons and a daughter whom he named Tamar, after the sister who had been wronged by Amnon. The sons are not named and likely died as young children, since later history notes that Absalom had no surviving sons to carry on his name.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern commentators see a contradiction between the three sons mentioned here and the later passage in chapter 18 where Absalom states he has no son.

notes.meaning: Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two entire years without being permitted to see the king. Being kept under house arrest without true reconciliation caused Absalom's anger and resentment to grow stronger.

Absalom sent for Joab twice to get him to plead his cause with David, but Joab refused to come each time. Joab likely stayed away because Absalom had not shown real gratitude for his earlier help and because Joab did not want to risk irritating the king.

Angry that Joab would not visit him, Absalom ordered his servants to burn down Joab's nearby field of ripe barley. His servants set the field ablaze, revealing Absalom's violent and lawless nature. He was willing to harm his own ally just to force an audience.
The fire got Joab's attention right away, and he rushed to Absalom's house to demand why his crops had been destroyed. Joab was furious over the loss of his property and wanted an explanation.

Absalom claimed he set the fire because Joab had ignored his calls for help. He stated that being trapped in Jerusalem was worse than being in exile and demanded an audience with David, daring the king to execute him if he was truly guilty. Absalom showed no repentance for Amnon's murder and felt completely justified in his past actions.

Joab reported Absalom's words to David, and the king finally summoned his son. Absalom bowed facedown before his father, and David welcomed him with a kiss of peace. By welcoming back an unrepentant son without any true change of heart, David set the stage for Absalom's later rebellion.
